chunks: I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the words of God, Blessed and Exalted: 'O you who believe! The testimony between you when death approaches one of you, at the time of making the will, is two just persons from among you, or two others from among others than you' [5:106]. I said, 'What are "two others from among others than you"?' He said, 'They are two unbelievers (kafirs).' I said, '"Two just persons from among you"?' So he said, 'Two Muslims.'

key_terms.ذَوَا عَدْلٍ: two just persons — witnesses of established moral uprightness (adalah) in Islamic law
key_terms.شَهَادَة: testimony/witnessing — the act of bearing witness in legal proceedings
key_terms.كَافِرَانِ: two unbelievers — non-Muslims whose testimony is exceptionally admissible in this Quranic ruling
key_terms.مُسْلِمَانِ: two Muslims — the default and preferred witnesses for Islamic legal testimony
key_terms.وَصِيَّة: bequest/will — a legal declaration made before death regarding one's estate and wishes

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about the Quranic verse 5:106 regarding witnesses for a bequest (wasiyya) at the time of death?
ai.summary: This hadith records Abu al-Sabbah al-Kinani's inquiry to Imam al-Sadiq (AS) about Quran 5:106, which addresses the witnessing of a bequest at the time of death. The Imam clarifies that 'two others from among others than you' (آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ) refers to non-Muslims (unbelievers), while 'two just persons from among you' (ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِنْكُمْ) refers to Muslims. This ruling is significant in Shia jurisprudence as it establishes that in exceptional circumstances — particularly during travel when Muslim witnesses are unavailable — the testimony of non-Muslims may be accepted for a dying person's bequest.
